justification: The passage locates the lift in “dense mats of fine root” found “in the few centimetres directly beneath the stones”, and Askerholt states: “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone.” That is exactly option B. A is contradicted because she does commit to a location; C overstates — half a metre down there was “almost nothing alive”, not entirely without roots; D (cut anchoring roots) is never mentioned.

Of the five failed streets the passage says: “They had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows” — option D verbatim. A fails because the roots rode “clear over the crates beneath”, i.e. the crates held; B confuses these five with the separate single street where “a water main was renewed”; C is directly contradicted by “The five had one thing in common.”

The trial “measure[s] the stones, and only the stones”, and Askerholt concedes: “For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength” — so the trial has no direct view beneath the successful streets (A). B is contradicted: the flags “stayed within tolerance” and the gauge “showed four millimetres”, i.e. some movement; C is an unwarranted absolute; D is never claimed.

The writer’s own verdict is the closing judgment: “The five streets are his, fairly won; the twenty-five are not” — Fearnbeck was right on one point (deep coarse bedding harbours roots) and wrong in his general prediction that “A celled pit buys time”, disproved on twenty-five of thirty streets. A misattributes Askerholt’s view (“had thought his worry overdone”) to the writer; C fails on the twenty-five; D fails because that closing sentence is the writer taking a side.

The text first explains why paving rises — the slab “builds the very thing that lifts it” — and then follows the celled-pavement trial through seven years of surveys, so C captures both halves. A is a single framing detail; B overstates a provisional result (“The stones are behaving; that is all I will sign my name to”); D is never proposed.

The frame is “it quietly takes its ___ on the general mood”; the only idiomatic collocation with ‘take ... on’ is “takes its toll on”. ‘Price’, ‘charge’ and ‘cost’ do not combine with ‘takes its ... on’ in standard English.

The sentence contrasts surface with substance: “The tone is light, but nobody misreads it; beneath the sponge the message is ___, and it is aimed at certain chairs.” Only ‘pointed’ supplies the needed contrast with ‘light’ and fits “aimed at certain chairs”, since a pointed message is one directed critically at particular people. ‘Relaxed’, ‘spirited’ and ‘amused’ would continue the lightness instead of undercutting it.

The gap completes the fixed idiom in “you cannot hold the moral high ___ and a dripping brush at the same time” — “the moral high ground”. ‘Field’, ‘horse’ and ‘floor’ (high horse would need ‘be on your high horse’, not ‘hold the moral high horse’) do not form the idiom.

“So the kitchen waits. ___, somebody cracks” needs a marker of time finally running out after a wait, which is ‘Eventually’. ‘Similarly’ has no parallel to point back to; ‘Presumably’ would hedge what the writer asserts as routine fact (“nearly always the same somebody”); ‘Ironically’ marks no irony present in the sentence.

The object is “an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor”, and the collocation for reaching such a compromise is “strike a balance”. ‘Casts’, ‘deals’ and ‘lands’ do not collocate with ‘balance’.

The passage states: “whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line” — option D restates this. A inverts it (the mortar “passes damp” to timber rather than sheltering it); B is contradicted because the tiles “hang from two small lugs at the head, the nibs, hooked over each batten”, not from the mortar; C overreaches — torching stopped only “the fine snow, dust and draughts” pushed up between the tiles, and wet still reached it.

The sequence supports B: “Six pews in the middle aisle are marked vacant that year, and four the year after”, and in the 1851 plan “the vacant marks are gone” precisely because “Thin ruled lines now cut the boxes into single sittings, let at two shillings apiece, and names crowd where one household’s name used to stand” — dividing the boxes filled pews that no longer let whole. A is contradicted by the preceding vacancies; C has no support, since nothing links the sittings to the free-bench poor; D misreads the price — two shillings bought one sitting (“apiece”), not a whole box.

Om släckningen säger texten: “Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl” — vilket är A. C förväxlar släckning med bränning, där “värmen [driver] ut koldioxiden ur stenen”; D strider mot att den släckta kalken först “blandad med sand ger murbruk”; B (göts i formar) nämns aldrig.

Texten är uttrycklig: “En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll. Den restes och brändes av ett ugnslag – en handfull grannar som sköt till var sin andel ved” — dvs. D. A motsägs av samma mening; B motsägs av att det var grannar, inte tillresta yrkesbrännare; C motsägs av “Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu.”

B täcker textens båda huvudlinjer: “för många hushåll var ugnen den binäring som över huvud taget gav kontanter” och lämningarna ligger kvar som “låga, övervuxna rösen av rödbränd sten” i landskapet. A motsägs av “Framför allt var det dit kalken gick: till murningen”; C är en överdrift utan stöd; D motsägs av att “Berget var däremot sällan något bekymmer” — ugnarna övergavs när skogen höggs ut och näringen förlorade sin marknad.

Slutsatsen i C följer av att resterna ofta ligger “flera i rad utmed samma sluttning, äldre ugnar som övergivits ... och ersatts av en yngre ugn längre bort” samt att “en och samma ugn som regel bara [brändes] vartannat eller vart tredje år” — antalet lämningar överdriver alltså hur många som var i gång samtidigt. A och B saknar varje jämförelse i texten, och D motsägs direkt av “Hur gamla de äldsta lämningarna är går inte att avgöra utan utgrävning.”

Svagheten i själva kalkylen är att “Kalkylen utgår ändå från de gamla lamporna” trots att kvicksilverlamporna “byttes ... mot ledbelysning” vintern 2023 — dvs. C. B beskriver ett annat fel i tjänsteskrivelsen (augustibesöket som stöd för “begränsat för flertalet motionärer”), inte kalkylen på 38 000; A påstås aldrig; D är bakvänt — författaren visar att besparingen är mindre än angivet, “omkring tolv tusen kronor”.

Författaren godtar sommarsläckningen — “för sommaren har nämnden faktiskt en poäng” — men kräver: “Släck vid nio på sommaren, håll tänt till elva från oktober till mars”, vilket är B. A motsägs av att han själv föreslår tidig släckning maj–augusti; C faller på att besparingen döms ut som liten, inte betydande; D är motsatsen till textens hela ärende.

Tennlövs resultat återges så: “Men där källorna är fylliga nog att pröva saken tycks årplatserna ofta ha fördelats efter gårdarnas mantal – de största hemmanen närmast aktern” — C återger både förbehållet (’där saken går att avgöra’) och mönstret. B motsäger förbehållet genom att utsträcka mönstret till socknar med knapphändiga protokoll; A vänder på orsaksriktningen; D (styrmansplats på omgång) förekommer inte i texten.

Författaren håller båda läsningarna öppna: “Samma rader kan alltså läsas som etikett eller som sjömanskap; protokollen skiljer inte mellan de två”, och han avstår uttryckligen från att välja: “Jag vet ärligt talat inte vad sätena visade” — dvs. B. A och C låter honom välja sida, vilket han inte gör; D anger fel skäl — hans tvivel gäller eftervärldens övertolkning (“läser in mer ordning än roddarna kände av”), inte tillrättalagda minnesbilder.

The passage states her team found “dense mats of fine root, thickening year on year” in “the few centimetres directly beneath the stones”, and quotes her: “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone.” Option C overstates (“almost nothing alive” is not “entirely without roots”), A is contradicted by her locating the force, and D’s cut anchoring roots are never mentioned.

The five failed streets “had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows”, matching D. C is contradicted (“The five had one thing in common”), B describes the separate single street with the renewed water main, and the crates never gave way — roots rode “clear over the crates beneath”.

The trial “measure[s] the stones, and only the stones”, and Askerholt says “We are reading the flags, not the roots … For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength.” So the trial has no direct view underground. B fails because flags “stayed within tolerance” and the gauge “showed four millimetres” — some movement occurred; C and D are unsupported.

The writer’s own closing verdict is “The five streets are his, fairly won; the twenty-five are not” — Fearnbeck was right about the five deep coarse-sand beds but wrong for the twenty-five that held. That evaluative sentence rules out D (she does take a side), C (“in full” fails on twenty-five streets), and A (“overdone” was Askerholt’s group’s view, which the five streets partly refuted).

The text first explains the mechanism — “The slab shades the ground, waters it every clear night and lets it breathe. It builds the very thing that lifts it” — then reports seven years of survey results on the celled remedy, mixed but promising. B’s “finally beat” overstates what Askerholt “will sign my name to”, A is only the opening frame, and D is never proposed.

The fixed idiom is “takes its toll”: the contest “quietly takes its toll on the general mood.” “Price” and “cost” collocate with “pay”/“count the cost”, not with “takes its … on”, and “takes its charge” is not English usage.

The sentence needs a contrast with “The tone is light, but nobody misreads it”, and “it is aimed at certain chairs” confirms a barbed message: “pointed”. “Relaxed”, “spirited” and “amused” would continue the cheerful surface rather than oppose it, defeating the “but”.

The idiom is “the moral high ground”: “you cannot hold the moral high ground and a dripping brush at the same time.” “Field”, “horse” (from “high horse”, which takes “on your”, not “hold the moral high”) and “floor” do not form the expression.

After “So the kitchen waits”, the needed link is temporal: “Eventually, somebody cracks”. “Similarly” has no parallel to draw, “Presumably” clashes with the writer’s confident “nearly always the same somebody”, and nothing ironic is being flagged.
The collocation is “strike a balance”: “most kitchens strike an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor.” “Cast”, “deal” and “land” do not collocate with “balance” in English.

The passage says “whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line”, which D restates. A claims the timber stayed sound, the opposite; B is contradicted because tiles “hang from two small lugs at the head, the nibs, hooked over each batten”; C overstates — torching stopped only “the fine snow, dust and draughts”, and “At that job it worked” limits the claim to that job.

Six middle-aisle pews were “marked vacant” in 1848 and four in 1849, and “In the plan of 1851 the vacant marks are gone” precisely when “Thin ruled lines now cut the boxes into single sittings” — the natural conclusion is that single lettings filled pews that would no longer let whole. A is undercut by those very vacancies, C speculates about poorer families with no textual support, and D misreads “two shillings apiece” per sitting as the price of a whole box.

The passage says of slaking: “Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl” — exactly A’s hissing apart into white powder. C describes the burning stage (“driver värmen ut koldioxiden ur stenen”), D fails because mortar required mixing “blandad med sand”, and casting in moulds is never mentioned.

The text states “En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll. Den restes och bränndes av ett ugnslag – en handfull grannar”, which is D. A contradicts the shared kiln, B contradicts “grannar” (neighbours, not travelling professionals), and C is contradicted by “Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu”.

The kilns were “den binäring som över huvud taget gav kontanter” and their traces persist as “ett sjuttiotal ugnsrester … låga, övervuxna rösen av rödbränd sten”, matching B. A is contradicted by “Framför allt var det dit kalken gick: till murningen”, D by “Berget var däremot sällan något bekymmer” (the market, not the stone, ran out), and C overstates the cash-income point into collapse.

The remains often lie “flera i rad utmed samma sluttning, äldre ugnar som övergivits … och ersatts av en yngre ugn längre bort”, and one kiln was fired only “vartannat eller vart tredje år” — so seventy remains overstate how many were running at once, which is C. D is directly contradicted (“går inte att avgöra utan utgrävning”), and neither a comparison with other districts (A) nor an earlier end than neighbouring parishes (B) is made.

The author’s attack on the calculation itself is that the old mercury lamps were replaced by LED in 2023 yet “Kalkylen utgår ändå från de gamla lamporna”, shrinking the true saving to about twelve thousand kronor — option C. B concerns the August head-count supporting the “begränsat för flertalet motionärer” claim, not the kalkyl, and its flaw is the season, not that it was a single visit; A is never raised; D inverts the direction — the kalkyl overstates, not understates.

The author concedes “för sommaren har nämnden faktiskt en poäng” and proposes “Släck vid nio på sommaren, håll tänt till elva från oktober till mars” — accept the cut in summer, reverse it in winter, exactly B. A is contradicted by the summer concession, C by the saving being merely “omkring tolv tusen kronor”, and D by the whole argument against the decision.

Tennlöv found that “där källorna är fylliga nog att pröva saken tycks årplatserna ofta ha fördelats efter gårdarnas mantal – de största hemmanen närmast aktern”, which C restates with its “där saken går att avgöra” qualifier. B extends the finding to parishes with scanty records, the opposite of that qualifier; A reverses cause and effect; D’s rotating helmsman’s seat appears nowhere — the styrmanstoft “krävde väderkännedom, inte anor”.

The author holds both readings open — “Samma rader kan alltså läsas som etikett eller som sjömanskap; protokollen skiljer inte mellan de två” — and ends “Jag vet ärligt talat inte vad sätena visade”, which is B. A and C each claim he settles the question, which he explicitly does not; D invents a reason (doctored recollections) absent from the text — his doubt rests on the sources’ silence and his own shifting reading.
